t: Minimum Consecutive Cards to Pick Up
o: Find the shortest contiguous subarray containing two cards of equal value; return its length, or −1 if all values are distinct. In Example 1 the closest repeated pair is either the two 3s (distance 4) or two 4s (distance 4), so the answer is 4. Example 2 has no repeats → −1. Only adjacent occurrences of the same value matter: the minimal window always spans two consecutive occurrences of some value.
k: The optimal window is always between two consecutive occurrences of the same value — tracking only the previous index of each value suffices.
One pass with a hash map from value → last seen index solves it in O(n).

a.n: Approach 1: Hash Map of Last Occurrence
a.i: Scan left to right storing the last index of each card value. When a value repeats at index i with previous index j, the window i−j+1 is a candidate; the global minimum over candidates is the answer because any matching pair spans at least the gap between consecutive occurrences.
s: Initialize an empty map and ans = ∞.
For each index i with value c: if c is in the map, update ans with i − last[c] + 1; set last[c] = i.
a.t: O(n) — single pass with O(1) average map operations.
a.sp: O(n) for the hash map in the worst case (all distinct).

a.i: Check every pair (i, j), i < j, and take the minimum j − i + 1 over pairs with equal values. Correct but quadratic — useful only as a baseline for tiny inputs.
s: Double loop over all index pairs.
Track the minimum window among equal-value pairs.

w: Always present the hash-map solution; the brute force is only a sanity baseline. Edge cases: exactly one duplicate pair anywhere, duplicates at the very start/end, and the all-distinct case returning −1. A common pitfall is computing j − i instead of j − i + 1. Follow-up: return the actual window, or handle a stream of cards.
